name: Quiet Ledger
thesis: One line per job, one page per job, one question per screen — and every number says how much it knows. Home is a ledger: an 11px LAST 24 HOURS label, one 34px verdict sentence, and beneath it rows that all share a single shape (3px state rail · identity · state phrase · a 14-run strip · size and cost), so "did my backups run?" is answered before you focus and "has this been quietly degrading?" is answered in the same glance. Every row links to the one page that owns the job whole — health, recovery, cost, settings, assumptions, history — and every long action reports where it was started, guarded server-side. Restore is a verb on that page, not a price on a chart, and it is branched honestly into the three recovery models the engine actually has (a snapshot repo you restore whole, a file catalog you restore one path at a time as-of a date, a prefix you warm up then download) with the exact `restore.sh` line for that job printed open beside the button, because the engine has to stay usable when the GUI is not. Trust is structural rather than asserted: measured is the quiet unmarked default, assumed is muted and dotted and physically barred from the largest type step, an observation from outside the model (bucket size, AWS invoice) is boxed like a receipt line, a projection inherits the weakest provenance of its inputs, and a forecast-vs-actual delta is printed only where the comparison is valid and suppressed with a printed reason where it is not. Severity splits on one axis that makes confusion impossible: a severity about a *configuration* sits inline beside the control that causes it, carries no timestamp and always carries a one-click fix; a severity about an *event* carries a time and a link to its record and never a fix button. And vocabulary is enforced typographically rather than editorially — mono means machine name, a machine name never appears without its plain-language half beside it, and a test in CI fails the build when either rule breaks. The surface is near-black and quiet; colour is spent on three things only: the rule under the verdict, the 3px rail on a row that needs you, and the run strip.

sitemap.name: Status
sitemap.question_it_answers: Did my backups run, is anything broken right now, and how bad would it be if this machine died?
sitemap.contents: LAST 24 HOURS label → one 34px verdict sentence with a 2px state-coloured rule → blockers that make data unrecoverable or unwritable (example passphrase, destination unreachable) → the job ledger, one row per job, sorted failed / running / overdue / clean-by-next-run / paused, each row carrying a 14-run strip and expanding in place on failure to the error's first line, the exit code, [Show output →] and [Back up now] → IF THIS MACHINE DIED TODAY (newest recoverable point per job, total hours, total dollars, what you will need — all from cached data, never a live repo call) → one cost line: forecast this month against the latest AWS invoice with a delta or a printed reason for its absence → [+ New job] and [Activity →]. While setup is incomplete, one 'Setup: 4 of 5 done' line sits directly under the verdict. Replaces today's 302 redirect and the /jobs config table.

sitemap.name: (redirect)
sitemap.contents: 301 to /. The brand link and old bookmarks keep working. There is no separate jobs destination, because Status is the jobs list.

sitemap.name: Job
sitemap.question_it_answers: How is this one job doing, how do I get its data back, what does it cost, and what is it set to?
sitemap.contents: The hub, and the only place a job is whole. Identity (name, composite kind token, source path → bucket prefix on one line). HEALTH from the state file, with the failure record inline when the last run failed (verbatim error, exit code, plain-language cause, the fix as a button) and [Back up now] / [Show output →]. GET IT BACK second on purpose: what exists to restore (cached count with its age, never a live repo call on page load), the honest warm-up cost of this job's class, [Restore…], [Test restore] with its price on its face, and the always-open shell fallback block carrying this job's exact restore.sh line. COST: typical month against measured-now with a delta, the four-line component breakdown, 'Show working ▸'. SETTINGS as read-only definition rows with one [Edit →]. ASSUMES as its own row with its own [Change ▸], because an assumption is not a setting. LAST 14 RUNS as the same strip, expanded into a table. [Delete this job] alone at the bottom behind a typed confirm.

sitemap.name: Run record
sitemap.question_it_answers: What happened in this exact run, and why did it fail?
sitemap.contents: One run as an addressable object: outcome, start, duration, exit code, restore point id where the type has one, the verbatim error, the job-tagged slice of the log, the command line that ran, and — for recognised error classes (source permission denied, repo lock held, thaw-required read, missing passphrase, empty source, bucket denied) — a 'Why this happens / What to do' pair with the fix as a button. Reached from every strip cell, every failure row, every flash and every Activity line. Failure is never terminal in the IA.

sitemap.name: Restore
sitemap.question_it_answers: How do I get this data back, what will it take, and what will it cost?
sitemap.contents: Three numbered questions, branched by job type because the engine has three incompatible recovery models. Snapshots (versioned): which restore point (top three from `restic snapshots --tag`, the rest behind a disclosure), what (everything / one path), where it lands. File history (versioned-files): which file (search the catalog), which version (latest, or 'as it was on <date>' → --asof), where it lands — with the honest statement that the engine restores one path at a time and the GUI queues them. Plain copy (archive): which folder under media/<job>/, warm up (tier picker), then download — two steps, not one. Below the questions: the cold-storage block with the real warm-up ceiling, the priced warm-up + download, and 'You can close this page.' Primary button named for what it actually starts. 'What this will need ▸' written for the worst day. The shell fallback for this job and type is printed open.

sitemap.name: Restore progress
sitemap.contents: One operation record persisted to disk (not in memory), so a container restart cannot make the interface lie: state, elapsed counter, the honest ceiling ('Warming up — 2h 14m elapsed; AWS Bulk allows up to 48 h'), objects thawed / total where the engine reports them, live output in a scrolling pane, and a [Download] button that stays disabled with its reason attached until the warm-up completes. Closing the page does not stop it; the job page and Activity both show the in-flight operation.

sitemap.name: New job
sitemap.question_it_answers: What do I want protected, what is the sensible way to protect it, and what will that cost?
sitemap.contents: Four numbered blocks opening in sequence. 1 Which folder — the confined tree, measured immediately on pick, the wait shown. 2 The plan — the comparison is OPEN by default with the recommendation pre-selected and its stated rule printed beside it: three type rows, then the storage-class table priced for THIS folder with five columns (class, $/mo, getting it back, minimum stay, cost to get it all back once), then how much changes, then how long to keep old versions. 3 How often — the preserved schedule builder with cross-job collision advice for snapshot jobs. 4 Name it. No sticky cost card: cost lives inside block 2 next to the controls that move it, and a 44px sticky footer carries [Create job], [Create and run it now], and exactly two figures on one axis.

sitemap.name: Edit job
sitemap.question_it_answers: What is this job set to, and what happens if I change it?
sitemap.contents: Same four blocks, all open, folder locked to the saved path with [Re-measure], name readonly. Every changed control shows its before-value inline and its consequence in place; changing the storage class raises the preserved advice pair unprompted (affects FUTURE uploads only; already-stored objects stay in the old class and warming them up to move them costs money). Assumptions round-trip from the saved job instead of resetting, so the estimate on edit cannot contradict the one approved at creation. A blocker disables Save, prints its reason under the button, offers one-click fixes, and offers a logged override that is recorded on the job.

sitemap.name: Recover
sitemap.question_it_answers: If this machine died, what could I get back, how long would it take, and what would it cost?
sitemap.contents: A top-level nav slot, written for future-you on a fresh machine. One row per job: what it protects, the newest recoverable point (cached, with its age), how many points exist and what kind they are, whether a warm-up is needed and for how long, retrieval + download cost, and what you will need — 'the repository passphrase' in plain words with RESTIC_PASSWORD in mono beside it. Per-type honesty is on the row, not in a footnote: a Plain copy row says 'current copy only — no version history'. Totals at the bottom. Every row ends in [Restore from this job →]. Nothing on this page issues a live repo call.

sitemap.name: Cost
sitemap.question_it_answers: What will this cost, when, and is the estimate right?
sitemap.contents: The one wider page (1180px). A segmented control picks the WHEN axis (First bill / Typical month / First 12 months / 24-month total); the matrix rows are the WHOSE axis (each job, then All jobs below a rule); the money column header names the held-constant axis in full, so no cell is ambiguous and none is missing. Size and storage class are editable inside the row, immediately left of the number they move; per-row consequence chips (minimum-stay lock-in with its worked example, per-object overhead) recompute with the row. Then OVER TIME, every curve labelled with its own end number. Then GETTING IT BACK, priced once per job with its warm-up time. Then three disclosures — Assumptions (persisted, with Apply to jobs / Reset to saved and a changed count), AWS invoice, How this is calculated — and exactly one price stamp. The Cost Explorer credential form is not on this page.

sitemap.name: Connect AWS billing
sitemap.question_it_answers: How do I let this app read my real S3 bill, and why does the tag matter?
sitemap.contents: The read-only Cost Explorer credential form, moved off /cost because it is setup, not cost. Write-only fields with the '••••• (unchanged)' placeholder, the separate-credential warning, and the cost-allocation tag field — with the plain statement that without a tag the invoice covers your whole AWS account, which is exactly why the delta is suppressed rather than shown wrong.

sitemap.name: Activity
sitemap.question_it_answers: What has this thing actually been doing, across all jobs?
sitemap.contents: The formerly orphaned log, now a page with a shell: the same ledger row for backups, restores, warm-ups, usage refreshes and provisioning runs, each tagged with its job, filterable by job and by outcome, each expanding to its log slice or linking to its run record. Long-running operations appear here live, which is how every slow action in the app reports progress.

sitemap.name: Setup
sitemap.question_it_answers: Is this machine actually able to back up — and able to restore?
sitemap.contents: A readiness checklist of real checks with a self-counting progress line ('4 of 5 done'), replacing the fictional 'Step 1 of 2' and the Provision/Config nav pair: destination reachable (the existing list→put→get→delete probe, with the date it last passed), repository passphrase set AND not the shipped CHANGEME value, bucket versioning on, at least one clean run, a rehearsed restore with its date. Each item is a ledger row with its own state, its own check method, its own timestamp and one action. Items that make data unrecoverable render as blockers here and are re-surfaced on Status. The LAN ONLY · NO LOGIN chip expands here into what an unauthenticated visitor on this network can actually do.

sitemap.name: Destination
sitemap.question_it_answers: Where do my backups go, and can this container write there?
sitemap.contents: The three preserved provisioning paths (guided-manual, scripted, automated) with their honest trust trade-offs, the real probe before anything is saved, transient admin credentials zeroed in a finally clause, scrubbed tool stderr in an open details. Adds a copy button on every block you are told to copy, re-renders the walkthrough and both credential fields intact on a validation failure, and ends every path — including the automated one — on the same next step: the passphrase.

sitemap.name: Keys & passphrase
sitemap.question_it_answers: Are the secrets set, and is the one that decides recoverability a real one?
sitemap.contents: Write-only secrets with per-key three-state status (set / not set / still the shipped example), the '••••• (unchanged)' placeholder, the 600-mode check, and the by-hand details block. The repository passphrase gets its own block at the top with the strongest copy in the app, computed by string-comparing against the known shipped placeholder rather than bool(value).

sitemap.name: Advanced settings
sitemap.contents: The raw env keys, grouped by what they are for (destination / recovery / billing / behaviour) with a one-line plain-language description each, reachable only from Setup. This is the one screen where the tool's own vocabulary is allowed to be primary.

sitemap.name: About & plain words
sitemap.question_it_answers: What version is this, and what does that word mean?
sitemap.contents: Version and build as a mono line, then 'Plain words for tool words' — the glossary anchor every mono token in the app dotted-underlines into (restic, rclone, repository, snapshot, catalog, prefix, tag, ingest, rotation, egress, thaw, GB-month, minimum storage duration, DEEP_ARCHIVE and the rest) — then the licence rows and the one sentence each about what restic, rclone and OpenTofu do for you.

sitemap.name: Something went wrong
sitemap.question_it_answers: What failed, did I lose what I typed, and what do I do?
sitemap.contents: The template behind all 14 abort() calls and any unhandled exception, carrying the shell: what was being attempted, the scrubbed message, what to try, [Back to Status] and the action that failed. Form validation never reaches here — a failing POST re-renders its own page with field-level messages and every value intact.

key_screens.layout:
One 960px column on near-black, centred, 2rem/1.5rem gutters. Topbar 56px: brand left, four nav items (Status / Recover / Cost / Setup), and at the far right the demoted no-auth notice as an 11px mono --faint chip reading LAN ONLY · NO LOGIN, linking to /setup — amber is no longer spent on permanent chrome. The page opens with the only large type in the app: an 11px mono caps label, a 34px verdict sentence, and a 2px full-bleed rule beneath it in the verdict's state colour. That rule is the single loud element on the screen. Then blockers if any, then the job ledger: full-width rows on 1px --border hairlines with a 3px status rail hard against the left edge (solid --ok clean, solid --danger failed, solid --warn overdue, 1.2s-sweeping --accent running, dashed --faint paused). The row is a five-column grid — rail 3px · identity 1fr · state phrase auto · run strip fixed 126px · numeric right-aligned 9ch — and the strip column is fixed so rows can never reflow. The strip is 14 runs, newest at the right, 6×14px cells with 2px gaps; the last 7 use saturated --ok/--danger/--warn and runs 8–14 use the derived dim tints, so recency reads loudest without changing meaning. A failed row grows in place; nothing navigates away to find out why. IF THIS MACHINE DIED TODAY is a bare section, built only from cached values. The cost line is one row, not a card. No cards, no tiles, no chart, no KPI row.

key_screens.interactions: Row click anywhere navigates to the job page; the two inline buttons on a failed row stop propagation. [Back up now] posts once, swaps to a working label with an elapsed counter, flips the rail to the sweeping accent, and is backed by a SERVER-side single-flight over the per-job lock that already exists — a second submit from a reload or another tab is refused with 'Already running since 05:00:12' rather than starting a duplicate. (That guard prevents double-submitting the SAME job; the shared-repo collision between two different snapshot jobs is a scheduling problem and is handled by the schedule builder's collision advice, never sold as the same fix.) Hovering a strip cell shows one line — date, outcome, duration, restore point id — and clicking it opens that run record. The page polls state files every 5s while anything is running and rewrites rails, phrases and elapsed counters in place with no layout shift; a cell that changes flashes --accent-bg for 200ms. OVERDUE is derived from the cron and last_run with a grace window of max(2× median duration, 1 hour) so a slow run or a clock skew cannot cry wolf; an overdue row reads 'Overdue — last ran 3 Jun, expected daily' and counts against the verdict. A paused job shows a dashed rail and 'Paused — not scheduled', never a live-looking cron. Delete is not on this screen at all. When more than six jobs exist the clean ones collapse behind one 'and 5 others ran clean' line that expands in place, with their strips still shown.

Settings: what it backs up with its measurement provenance and timestamp, when, where it is stored, what it keeps
Assumptions, visually separated from settings, dated, with their own change path
Last 14 runs: the same strip as Status, expanded into a table
Delete, alone, last
key_screens.interactions: Restore points are NOT fetched on page load — `restic snapshots` is a repo operation and this page must open instantly — so GET IT BACK shows the cached count with its age and the live list loads on the restore screen with a real loading row. [Test restore] pulls one small file to a scratch path, diffs it, deletes the scratch and writes its date into both this section and the Setup checklist; on a cold job it is not a button but a disclosure that states the true cost in hours before anything is spent. 'What a restore needs ▸' expands to four lines written for the worst day: the repository passphrase, the bucket and its key, the time, and the statement that this works on a machine where /mnt/user/appdata no longer exists — that is the point. 'Show working ▸' expands the model's derivation for this job only, in place, never navigating away. [Re-measure] runs the folder walk with a progress state and rewrites the measured line and its timestamp. Every mono token is a dotted-underline link to its glossary anchor. While a backup or restore is running, HEALTH becomes the live block with an elapsed counter and a streaming [Show output]. Strip cells and history rows both open the run record. The failure record's fix buttons are the only actions inside a retrospective severity block, and they are actions on the job, not on the block.

key_screens.layout:
Same 960px column, four numbered blocks with mono caps labels, plus a 44px sticky FOOTER — the sticky element is the footer, never a cost header, so the controls can never scroll under their own output and Create is always reachable. Blocks 2–4 are dimmed to --faint with the reason printed in place until a folder is picked, because every recommendation below depends on the measurement; the dependency is taught, not concealed. Block 2 is where the winning direction's one weakness is corrected: the comparison is OPEN by default with the recommendation pre-selected and marked, not collapsed behind a disclosure — the owner's complaint was that the wizard was confusing about what to choose and why, which is a comprehension problem, not a decision-fatigue one. The recommendation is offered only when a stated rule fires and the rule is printed; when no rule fires nothing is pre-selected and the block says so. Cost lives inside block 2, next to the controls that move it, in two sentences — there is no growing sticky card anywhere. One line at the top of the page states the three idioms once.

Empty state — one sentence and one button, never a numbered list of things you still have to do
Error page and inline field errors — forms re-render themselves with values intact; the error page is the last resort
visual_system.severity_scale: Six levels on two axes, and the axis split is what makes them impossible to confuse. PROSPECTIVE severities describe a configuration: they render inline beside the control that causes them, they never carry a timestamp, and they always carry a one-click fix. RETROSPECTIVE severities describe an event: they always carry a time and a link to a record, and the only buttons inside them are actions on the job, never on the block. Each level is encoded on four channels at once — left rule weight, glyph, fill, and an 11px mono caps tab — so severity survives greyscale and is never a hue you have to decode. Prospective: (1) NOTE — no rule, no glyph, no fill, 13px --faint; the absence of marking is itself the lowest level, which is what makes the others legible. (2) RECOMMENDED — 2px --accent rule, '→' glyph, tab RECOMMENDED, no fill; it always carries a button that applies it, because advice that cannot be taken in one click is just prose. (3) HEADS UP — 2px --warn rule, --warn-bg fill, '!' glyph, tab HEADS UP; real money and real time only (minimum-stay lock-in, warm-up waits, a class change affecting future uploads only, per-object overhead), never chrome. (4) WON'T RUN — 3px --danger rule, --danger-bg fill, '✕' glyph, tab WON'T RUN; it disables the primary button, prints its reason under it, offers the fix as buttons that set the fields for you, and offers a 'Save it anyway ▸' override that is recorded on the job — so a predicate that turns out to be wrong for a MinIO or non-AWS endpoint is a speed bump rather than a hard wall the owner patches out. Retrospective: (5) DONE — 2px --ok rule, --ok-bg fill, '✓' glyph, tab DONE, always with a time; the success style that did not previously exist. (6) FAILED — 3px --danger rule, --danger-bg fill, '✕' glyph, tab FAILED, always with a time and an exit code, and structurally it must carry two links, 'Show output →' and the action that failed, so failure is never terminal in the IA. Flashes are typed at the call site into levels 3, 5 and 6; the single accent box that served success and error alike is gone. The permanent amber 'No authentication' strip is demoted to an 11px mono --faint topbar chip reading LAN ONLY · NO LOGIN that expands on /setup into one real HEADS UP row naming what an unauthenticated visitor can now actually do — which is what frees --warn to mean something everywhere else.
visual_system.provenance_marks: Three textures applied to the number itself rather than to a badge beside it, so provenance travels with the figure into tables, sentences and headlines — plus one inheritance rule and one type-scale rule that do most of the work. MEASURED / PROJECTED is unmarked: plain mono --ink, tabular. The trustworthy state is the quiet one and it is the only one allowed to be quiet; its title and its sub-line carry the stamp ('533 files · measured today 05:02'). ASSUMED is --muted with a 1px dotted underline at 3px offset, the word 'assumed' beneath it in any table, and a title naming the guess and its source ('20 GB is a placeholder, not a measurement. Run this job once to measure it.'). OBSERVED is a boxed mono receipt cell — 1px --border-strong, --surface-2 fill — reserved for values that come from outside the model: 'Measured now' (rclone size priced at today's rates) and 'AWS invoice' (Cost Explorer), each labelled by its column header and stamped with its age. The INHERITANCE RULE makes the system computable rather than decorative: a projected figure inherits the weakest provenance of its inputs and says so, so a monthly cost built on an assumed size renders muted and dotted, and measuring the folder turns the same figure plain and bright without a word changing. The TYPE-SCALE RULE makes it enforceable by layout: an assumed figure is barred from the 34px step and drops one step, so an unmeasured 1.78 TB folder cannot present a confident headline. Two derived marks complete it. The DELTA CHIP is rendered only where a forecast and a comparable actual sit in the same row — mono ±n%, --ok within 10%, --warn beyond — and is SUPPRESSED, with a printed one-line reason in its place, when no cost-allocation tag makes the comparison valid, because a large meaningless delta would discredit a model that is correct to about 1%. The PRICE STAMP appears exactly once per money-bearing screen, at the bottom, rendering price_source and price_date verbatim, so 'bundled table, captured 2026-08-01' and 'live AWS price list, fetched 15 Sep 09:04' are finally distinguishable instead of living only inside the model. And where the engine cannot produce a per-job observation — all snapshot jobs share one store, and Cost Explorer has no per-prefix breakdown — the interface says so on the row rather than inventing a split: two or more snapshot jobs merge into one 'snapshot store, measured together' row, and the invoice lives only on the All-jobs row.
visual_system.motion: Four uses, no more, all disabled under prefers-reduced-motion (the existing global rule is kept). (1) The running rail: a 1.2s linear sweep along the 3px bar — the only continuously animated pixel in the app, and the only in-progress indication that needs no text. (2) The recompute flash: any figure that changes during a live recalculation gets a 200ms --accent-bg fade on its own cell. This is the fix for cause and effect never being visible together: it makes the causal link something you watch land rather than something the copy asserts, and on the cost matrix it makes clear which of a dozen figures your lever actually moved. (3) Disclosure expansion: 120ms ease-out height, enough to show that content pushed in rather than that the page jumped. (4) The strip landing: when a run completes while you are watching, the newest cell fades in over 200ms and the older cells shift left — the one place a layout change is the message. No page transitions, no skeleton shimmer, no hover lifts, no shadows, no scroll-triggered reveals; progress buttons change their label and gain an elapsed counter rather than spinning. Under reduced motion the sweep becomes a static striped bar with a counting 'working… 12s' label, the flash becomes a static 2px --accent left rule held for 2s, and the disclosure and the strip snap.

problem_resolutions.how_resolved: /jobs/<name> exists and is the object. One page owns identity (both addresses on one line — /mnt/user/appdata → s3://bw-backups/appdata/, tag appdata), health from the state file, recovery, forecast, measured spend, settings, assumptions and run history, in that order. The job NAME becomes the single identifier and always links here: from the Status row, the cost matrix (re-keyed from the raw engine string and the S3 'Prefix' column to the job name, with the prefix demoted to a mono sub-line), the Recover table, every Activity line and every flash. That re-keying is the mechanical change that lets a forecast and a real measurement for the same job finally sit in one row with a delta between them. Runs become addressable objects at /jobs/<name>/runs/<run_id>, reached from every strip cell, every failure row and every log line, so 'what exactly ran' has a URL. Status stops being a config table and becomes a roll-up of these pages.

Restore is the second section of every job page — above cost, above settings — and a real route that drives the existing scripts/restore.sh dispatch rather than reimplementing it. Crucially it is BRANCHED, because the engine has three incompatible recovery models and the winning pitch drew only one: Snapshots gets a point-in-time list and a whole-tree restore; File history gets a catalog search, a version picker ('as it was on 1 June' → --asof) and the honest statement that the engine restores one path at a time while the GUI queues them; Plain copy gets a prefix picker, a warm-up step with a tier and a real waiting state, then a separate download step — because `restore.sh <archive-job> list` does not exist. Every branch prints that job's exact restore.sh invocation OPEN with a copy button, framed as 'the GUI is a convenience; the engine restores without it.' The cold-storage truth is a HEADS UP block between the questions and the button, carrying the class, the real ceiling ('Bulk, up to 48 h'), the tier picker and the priced warm-up plus download; the primary button is named for what it actually starts. /recover answers the whole-machine question for all jobs at once, and 'IF THIS MACHINE DIED TODAY' puts the same answer on Status. Full-restore cost stops being a hero KPI divorced from a feature and appears in exactly three places where it is a decision: inside the plan at creation, inside GET IT BACK on the job page, and in the workbench's GETTING IT BACK band where every row ends in a link to the action it prices.

The 2×2 is drawn as a 2×2. /cost is one matrix: rows are the WHOSE axis (each job, then an All jobs row below a rule), a single segmented control is the WHEN axis (First bill / Typical month / First 12 months / 24-month total), and the money column header names the held-constant axis in full, so no cell is ambiguous and none is missing. 'FIRST BILL / THIS JOB / MO / NEW TOTAL / MO' as three unlabelled cells is deleted. The wizard's sticky footer holds WHEN constant and shows a complete ROW of the matrix under the same two words — 'a typical month — this job $2.69 · all jobs $4.54' — so the number approved at creation is findable later by the name it was approved under, and the surface that showed three of four cells now shows a labelled row rather than a fourth cell nobody needs. Keep-everything is honoured identically on both surfaces and on the curve: 'still growing' replaces the typical-month qualifier, 'at least' prefixes the 12- and 24-month totals, and the timeline prints the honest sentence ('manga keeps everything it has ever copied, so its line never plateaus'). The plateau the model explicitly flags as unreal is never printed as if it were.

Expressed as arrangement first and copy second. 'How much of it changes each backup?' is asked in the owner's own terms and placed immediately ABOVE 'How long to keep old versions', inside the same block, so cause and effect are never separated by scroll. Each keep-rule option shows its own live +$/mo under the assumption above it, and the consequence is stated prospectively in place: at ~1% churn, 'old versions settle at about 1.22× your data — $1.48 of the $2.69'; at 0%, every option reads +$0.00 with 'nothing gets replaced, so there are no old versions to store' attached. The defending paragraph asserting the settings 'correctly have no cost effect' is deleted, because the arrangement now says it. But the control is NOT removed at 0% churn, which is where the winning pitch over-corrected: retention bounds how far back you can restore and how much one bad night can cost you, and suppressing a recovery-relevant setting on a cost argument is a category error. Instead the block header reads 'no cost effect at 0% change — still bounds how far back you can restore', the options go --muted, and the panel is visibly inert without being absent.

No growing sticky hero anywhere. The wizard's unbounded pinned cost card is replaced by two things: cost sentences that live INSIDE block 2, next to the controls that move them, and a 44px sticky FOOTER of fixed height carrying Create, Cancel and exactly two same-axis figures — so the form can never scroll under its own output and Create is always reachable. On /cost the levers move inside the result: each row's size and storage class are editable cells immediately left of the number they move. The two panels that could not recompute are not restyled but deleted and rebuilt as things that do — the M1/M6/M12/M24 milestones table becomes the WHEN segmented control over the same matrix, and the cold-storage lock-in list becomes a per-row chip recomputing with its row — under the stated constraint that a panel which cannot recompute does not belong on a live page. And the recompute is made observable: every changed cell flashes --accent-bg for 200ms, so 'change anything and every number updates live' is watched rather than claimed.

Three kinds of value, three idioms, three persistence rules, stated once at the top of the create/edit page and never repeated. SETTINGS are form controls, saved through jobs_io, and rendered on the job page as read-only definition rows with one [Edit →]. MEASURED FACTS are never controls: read-only figures with their own timestamp and a [Re-measure] action ('52.71 GB · 533 files · measured today 05:02'). ASSUMPTIONS are marked as assumptions, labelled 'these describe your data, not your backups', and — the fix — PERSISTED into jobs.json as an `assumptions` sub-object (change_rate_pct, bundled, restore_fraction, restores_per_year, retrieval_tier, set_at) with a migration that backfills defaults, because jobs_io.validate currently constructs its output dict fresh and silently drops exactly these keys. They round-trip on edit, so the edit screen's estimate can no longer contradict the one approved at creation, and they appear on the job page as their own ASSUMES section, visually separated from settings, dated, with its own [Change ▸]. Every what-if on /cost is applyable ([Apply to jobs]), resettable ([Reset to saved]) and diffed (a changed count), so a throwaway can become a decision or be undone and is never mistaken for a setting.

Every number states where it came from, in its own rendering rather than in a badge: measured and projected are plain mono --ink with a timestamped stamp (the trustworthy state is the quiet one); assumed is --muted with a dotted underline, the word 'assumed' in tables, and a title naming the guess and its source; an observation from outside the model — 'Measured now' from rclone size, 'AWS invoice' from Cost Explorer — is a boxed mono receipt cell. Two rules make it computable instead of decorative: a projected figure INHERITS THE WEAKEST PROVENANCE OF ITS INPUTS, and an assumed figure is BARRED FROM THE 34px TYPE STEP, so an unmeasured 1.78 TB folder physically cannot present a confident headline. price_source and price_date, which exist in the model and are rendered nowhere today, become exactly one price stamp per money-bearing screen, so 'bundled table, captured 2026-08-01' and 'live AWS price list, fetched 15 Sep 09:04' are finally distinguishable. And the cheapest trust win is built with the scope the engine actually has: forecast against measured-now per job where a per-job prefix exists (media/<job> for Plain copy and File history), forecast against the shared snapshot store where it does not, and the AWS invoice only on the All-jobs row — because Cost Explorer returns one account-or-tag amount per month and has no per-prefix breakdown. The delta chip is suppressed with a printed reason wherever no cost-allocation tag makes the comparison valid.

One severity scale, six levels, four encoding channels each (rule weight, glyph, fill, mono caps tab) — and a prospective/retrospective axis that makes guidance and outcome structurally unconfusable: a configuration severity renders beside its control, carries no timestamp and always carries a one-click fix; an event severity carries a time and a link to its record and contains no fix button. NOTE is unmarked; RECOMMENDED always carries a button that applies it; HEADS UP is spent only on real money and real time; WON'T RUN disables the primary, prints its reason under the button, offers fixes that set the fields for you, and offers a logged override recorded on the job so a wrong predicate is a speed bump rather than a wall the owner patches out. Incompatible classes stay visible in the table, struck through with the reason in the cell, because removing them teaches nothing. DONE and FAILED are outcome styles with timestamps that share no component with advice at all, replacing the single accent-blue flash that served success and error alike, and FAILED must structurally carry two links so failure is never terminal.

Status is a status board. Every row renders the state file the engine already writes — outcome as a phrase with its time attached, duration, next scheduled run, size, and on failure the error's first line, the exit code and a plain-language cause inline with [Show output →] and [Back up now]. Three additions close the remaining gaps. A 14-RUN STRIP on every row, so an intermittently failing job cannot hide behind last night's success — this needs run history, which does NOT exist today (backup-job.sh overwrites state/<job>.json each run), so the direction budgets it explicitly as its one engine change: append one JSON line to state/<job>.jsonl at the two points that already write the state file. An OVERDUE state derived from the cron and last_run with a grace window of max(2× median duration, 1 hour), so a schedule that silently stopped in June reads 'Overdue — last ran 3 Jun, expected daily', sorts to the top and counts against the verdict, without crying wolf on a slow run or a clock skew. And PAUSED rendered from the persisted enabled flag that was never displayed, so a paused job stops advertising a live-looking cron. In-progress is a real state: a sweeping rail, an elapsed counter, streaming output, and a SERVER-side single-flight over the existing per-job lock that refuses a second submit with 'Already running since 05:00:12'. (That guard stops double-submitting the same job; the shared-repo collision between two different snapshot jobs is a scheduling problem, handled by the schedule builder's different-minute advice, and the two are never sold as the same fix.) Failure is never a dead end: every badge, flash and strip cell links to /jobs/<name>/runs/<run_id>, which gives the verbatim error, the exit code, the command line, the log slice and a cause/fix pair for recognised error classes.

'First-time setup · Step 1 of 2' is deleted along with the idea of an announced sequence the app cannot keep. /setup is a readiness checklist of real checks with a self-counting progress line ('4 of 6 done') that cannot be wrong: destination reachable via the preserved list→put→get→delete probe with the date it last passed; repository passphrase set AND not the shipped example; bucket versioning on; at least one clean run; a rehearsed restore with its date; and what no-login actually means now that this app can spend money and write files. 'Set up' stops being a boolean — the passphrase check string-compares against the shipped CHANGEME placeholder and, while they match, renders as a BLOCKER on both /setup and Status: 'Still the shipped example value. Anything backed up with it can be read by anyone who has this image, and changing it later will not re-encrypt what is already stored.' The restore rehearsal is a real drill, not a checkbox: it restores the smallest restore point of the cheapest warm job to a scratch path, diffs a file, deletes the scratch and records the date, with its cost shown before it starts and an honest refusal (with the true hours) on a cold-only install. All four provisioning exits, including the automated one, return here, so 'what next' has one answer instead of three contradictory flashes; Provision and Config both leave the top nav; and the Jobs empty state becomes one sentence and one button.

One name per concept, applied identically across Status, the job page, the wizard, the cost matrix, Recover, Restore and Activity — and demoted by a typographic law rather than by editorial discipline. Mono means machine name; a human word is never set in mono; a machine name never appears WITHOUT its plain-language half adjacent to it (composite tokens: 'Snapshots · versioned', 'Deepest · DEEP_ARCHIVE'); and every mono token is a dotted-underline link to /about#plain-words. The rule is enforced by a pytest over the templates that fails the build when a machine-name term appears outside a mono span or a mono span contains a word not on the list — which is what keeps it from eroding in a few commits. Two naming traps are avoided deliberately: the archive type is 'Plain copy', not 'Mirror', because jobs_io persists a real `mirror` boolean on archive jobs and a non-mirror archive job is legal; and 'archive' is retired as a type name because it collides with the storage-class word. restic, rclone, catalog, prefix, ingest, rotation, egress and thaw get plain replacements with the original always one click away — and the constants the owner will meet outside the GUI, in jobs.json, in the log, in backup-job.sh and in the AWS console, stay on screen rather than being hidden, because the point is to demote the translation table, not to move it to the boundary.

The shell gets the three vocabularies it lacked. SEVERITY: the six-level prospective/retrospective scale above, with flashes typed at the call site — a real DONE style, a FAILED style that structurally carries links, a HEADS UP style — instead of one accent box for success and error alike. PROGRESS: every long action uses the progress button — it swaps to a working label with an elapsed counter, disables its twin, writes a live row into Activity, and is backed by a server-side single-flight — applied to Back up now, restore, warm-up, Refresh usage, Test & Validate and Provision now, so 'Provision now' running tofu init + apply for minutes and 'Refresh usage' running rclone size both report where the button is rather than five sections above it, and neither can be double-submitted into 'bucket already exists'. Long-running operations persist their record to disk, so a container restart cannot leave the interface confidently describing a warm-up nobody is tracking. FAILURE CONTAINMENT: validation is per-field on blur and, on submit, a server-side rejection re-renders the same page with field-level messages and every value intact, so a double space in a hand-typed cron can no longer discard the app's longest form; the 14 abort() calls and any unhandled exception land on a real error template carrying the shell, the plain cause and the action that failed. And the permanent amber 'No authentication' strip becomes an 11px mono --faint topbar chip that expands on /setup into one real HEADS UP row naming what an unauthenticated visitor can now actually do — which is what gives --warn back its meaning everywhere else.

risks: Run history does not exist and this direction depends on it. backup-job.sh writes a single JSON object to state/<job>.json and overwrites it every run, so the 14-run strip, the last-14-runs table, /jobs/<name>/runs/<run_id>, duration-vs-median and the OVERDUE grace window all require a new append-only per-job store. The budget is deliberately minimal — append one JSON line to state/<job>.jsonl at the two points that already write the state file, plus a reader that tails the last N and a size cap — but it IS engine work, it is not free, and no part of this direction should be pitched as already-written data. If it is cut, the strip must be cut with it rather than faked from one row.

Restore is the app's first operation that spends money and writes to the filesystem at a user-chosen path, on a surface that ships with no authentication. Confinement under RESTORE_ROOT via the existing safe_resolve gate, outright refusal of any target inside a job's source, and server-side traversal rejection are the right guards — but demoting the auth banner to a faint chip buys visual quiet at exactly the moment the stakes of that banner rise. The mitigation is the HEADS UP row on /setup naming what an unauthenticated visitor can do; if this is ever reachable beyond the LAN, the trade is wrong regardless.

Warm-up is asynchronous and measured in hours, with no daemon behind the GUI. The operation record is persisted to disk and the page says it lost track rather than guessing when a record exceeds its tier's ceiling with no completion — but an interface that lies about state is worse than one that never showed it, and getting this right across container restarts is the largest single build cost in the direction after run history.

OVERDUE is computed from a 5-field cron compared against last_run, which is logic that does not exist today. A timezone or DST mismatch turns a healthy install red, and a board that cries wolf once is ignored forever after. The grace window of max(2× median duration, 1 hour) mitigates it; a cron parsing bug does not degrade gracefully, because it makes the largest sentence in the app say something false.

Persisting assumptions into jobs.json changes the schema and forces jobs_io.validate to grow an `assumptions` object plus a migration for existing files. If the migration is skipped, the fix for problem 6 silently regresses into exactly the bug it was meant to solve — assumptions that reset on edit — and the edit screen resumes contradicting the estimate the owner approved.

Per-job cost truth is bounded by what the engine can observe. Snapshot jobs share one appdata/ prefix so their 'measured now' cannot be split per job, and Cost Explorer returns one account-or-tag amount per month with no per-prefix breakdown, so the AWS invoice can only ever live on the All-jobs row. The interface states both limits on the row rather than inventing a split — which is honest, but it means the strongest trust element is weakest exactly where the owner has more than one snapshot job.

The delta is absent by default. It is suppressed without a cost-allocation tag, which most owners will not set, so the single best trust-building element on the cost page appears only after an optional setup step — and an owner who sets a tag mid-history will see the delta jump for reasons that have nothing to do with the model.

The type recommendation in block 2 is offered only when a stated rule fires and the rule is printed, which is the correction to the winning pitch's accepted-by-default plan — but a printed rule is still a heuristic reading size, file count and mtime distribution. It will be wrong for sparse VM images and for datasets edited in place, and storage class only affects future uploads, so a wrong plan is expensive to undo. If a case cannot be given a truthful one-sentence rule, no recommendation should be made for that case and the block must say so.

The mono-means-machine-name law is only as strong as its lint. The pytest that enforces it is a grep over templates with an allowlist, which will need maintenance and will produce false positives on new copy; if it is disabled once under deadline pressure, the rule erodes silently and the vocabulary fix regresses to editorial discipline, which is what failed the first time.

The cost matrix earns its own 1180px container, which is the direction's only exception to a single page width, and that exception will be argued about. At four or more jobs with provenance and consequence sub-lines it is still tall enough that the total may fall below the fold, which partly undoes the minimalism that justifies the rest of the app.

Branching restore into three shapes triples the surface of the most consequential screen in the app and means two of the three branches are built for job types the owner may not have. The always-open shell fallback is the honest hedge — it works for all three on day one — but if only the Snapshots branch ships, the app will silently be least useful for exactly the job type (Plain copy on Deep Archive) where recovery is hardest.

The restore drill is the strongest trust-builder here and the most expensive to build honestly. Shipped as a dry run that does not actually read bytes back from S3 and diff them, it becomes theatre on the one screen whose entire job is to stop the app lying about readiness.

judge_summary:
Two of three judges picked Quiet Ledger (36 and 34); the third picked Runbook (36) with Quiet Ledger at 31.5. Night Shift placed third on every card. So the base is Quiet Ledger, and the arbitration is between its two weak spots and Runbook's two strengths.

What all three judges agreed on. (a) Every direction resolved all 12 problems with mechanisms rather than assertions; the separation was craft-per-unit-of-build and factual accuracy against the engine. (b) Night Shift's centrepiece — the 30-night ledger and the per-timestamp run record — rests on run history that does not exist, and it claimed the opposite ('fields already being written and never shown'); two judges called that overclaim disqualifying, and the third scored its buildability 4/10. Its run strip is still the best glance artifact anyone proposed. (c) All three flagged Quiet Ledger's accepted-by-default recommended plan as its worst idea for this owner, whose complaint was comprehension, not decision fatigue. (d) Two of three flagged that deleting the retention control at 0% churn is a category error, because retention bounds the restore window, not only the bill. (e) Two of three flagged that Quiet Ledger's flagship restore mock draws restic-shaped restore points for a job it labels versioned-files — the most consequential specification error in an otherwise accurate direction. (f) Judge 3 verified against the code that Runbook's per-job AWS invoice cannot be produced (Cost Explorer is account-or-tag only, with no per-prefix breakdown; and all versioned jobs share one measured prefix), and that Runbook's 264px margin column on fourteen Jinja templates degrades into Quiet Ledger's single column anyway. (g) All three noted that the Run-now guard does not prevent the shared-repo collision, which is a scheduling problem between two different snapshot jobs.

How I resolved it. I kept Quiet Ledger's skeleton unchanged — one ledger row reused across six screens, one reserved 34px step, provenance enforced by hierarchy rather than decoration, levers inside the rows, server-side single-flight — because that is what lets one developer finish the whole redesign rather than 70% of it, and because judge 3 verified its cost data model is the only one that matches what the code exposes. Then four corrections: the plan block ships OPEN with Runbook's priced five-column class table and a recommendation that is pre-selected only when a stated rule fires and the rule is printed; retention survives at 0% churn with Runbook's non-cost justification; restore is branched into the three recovery models the engine actually has, each with Runbook's always-open shell fallback; and 'Mirror' becomes 'Plain copy' because jobs_io persists a real `mirror` boolean on archive jobs. Then three grafts that cost almost nothing and close the winner's only gap on the Tuesday-morning question: Night Shift's run strip (as 14 runs, not nights), its OVERDUE derived state (with a grace window I added), and its prospective/retrospective severity axis. Runbook's mono law is adopted with the enforcement Runbook admitted it lacked. Night Shift's margin-free, rule-separated sectioning was already Quiet Ledger's, so nothing was borrowed there. The two things I refused to graft are Runbook's margin column (it is the most expensive recurring commitment in the set and its own fallback is this layout) and any per-job AWS invoice figure (it cannot be built).

The honest cost of the synthesis: it commits to one engine change the winning direction did not budget — an append-only run history — plus a jobs.json assumptions migration and a persisted operation record for warm-ups. All three are named in the risks rather than hidden in a layout claim, which is precisely the failure that cost Night Shift the win.
